name: Eye color change surgery (keratopigmentation / iris implants)

image.caption: Eye color change surgery (keratopigmentation / iris implants)

lead: Two kinds of procedure aim to change the apparent colour of healthy eyes: cosmetic iris implants, such as NewColorIris and BrightOcular, which are silicone discs placed in front of the natural iris, and keratopigmentation, which tints the cornea. The payoff people want is a different eye colour, visible as soon as the procedure is done.

Implants cover the natural iris with a coloured disc, while keratopigmentation deposits pigment in corneal layers, with femtosecond lasers used in newer versions. Published literature on cosmetic iris implants is largely case reports and case series. A 2023 review states that iris implants were designed for conditions such as aniridia and are not approved by regulators anywhere for cosmetic use in healthy eyes.

paras: Both are eye surgeries done by ophthalmic surgeons, often abroad, with the colour change visible once the eye heals. Some people consider coloured contact lenses as a non-surgical alternative.

Reported problems include corneal decompensation or damage, raised eye pressure and glaucoma, inflammation and vision loss. Cosmetic iris implants are not approved by regulators anywhere, and vision-threatening complications are the main finding in the literature.

angle.text: An implant or corneal pigment changes the apparent colour of the iris, so the colour shift is visible once the procedure is done. Published reports mainly document complications, and cosmetic iris implants are not approved by regulators.

lead: Eye color change surgery refers to procedures intended to alter the apparent color of healthy eyes, most often to turn dark brown eyes light blue, green or hazel. People pursue it because iris color is one of the most noticeable features of the eye area, and a lighter or more striking iris is widely discussed in appearance communities as a way to change the impression of the whole face. Two approaches are discussed: cosmetic iris implants, such as NewColorIris and BrightOcular, which are placed inside the eye in front of the natural iris, and keratopigmentation, in which pigment is deposited in the cornea [1].

Keratopigmentation (corneal tattooing) has a long history as a way of masking corneal scars. Modern femtosecond-laser versions, described from about 2011 for iris atrophy and from the mid-2010s for purely cosmetic colour change, have grown in visibility on social media [1][2][3]. Reviews of keratopigmentation describe a mix of therapeutic and cosmetic use, with reports of good outcomes in selected patients alongside calls for longer-term data on purely cosmetic cases [2][3][4].

Published literature on cosmetic iris implants consists largely of case reports and case series describing complications including corneal decompensation, raised eye pressure, inflammation and vision loss [5]. A 2023 review states that iris implants were designed for conditions such as aniridia and are not approved by regulators anywhere for cosmetic use in healthy eyes. Tinted contact lenses, the removable alternative, are the most common route to a different eye colour and are frequently compared with surgery in forum discussions [6].
infobox: Iris implants not approved for cosmetic use anywhere, per a 2023 review
BrightOcular described as removable [1]; keratopigmentation difficult to control [1]
About $12,000, per a 2024 Allure article cited by Wikipedia [1]

paras: Iris color depends on the amount of melanin in the pigmented layer at the back of the iris and in the front stroma, together with the density of the stromal cells. Blue, green and hazel eyes look that way because of how light scatters in the stroma rather than because of blue or green pigment [7]. Eye color is polygenic; the OCA2 and HERC2 genes on chromosome 15 account for much of the variation, and a specific HERC2 variant is strongly associated with blue eyes [7].

Brown is the most common color, found in roughly 79% of people worldwide, against about 8 to 10% blue, 5% hazel, 3% gray and 2% green [7]. This distribution is the backdrop to interest in surgery: people with dark brown eyes are the main audience for procedures that produce lighter shades [6].

Iris implants were first described for treating photophobia and glare from aniridia, coloboma and other iris defects; the same devices have been used cosmetically in healthy eyes. The wider field of prosthetic irises goes back to the 1960s, when Peter Choyce developed a prosthetic iris in PMMA; foldable silicone irises were designed from the early 2000s by HumanOptics with Hans Reinhard Koch, and the HumanOptics CustomFlex was cleared by the US FDA in 2018 for iris defects [8]. Wikipedia notes that ophthalmologists criticise cosmetic use of such devices in healthy eyes because of the risk of vision loss [8].

Cosmetic implants of the NewColorIris type are reported to have a record of high ocular morbidity and are no longer in use. A newer BrightOcular design added grooves intended to lessen iris contact and permit fluid flow around the implant. Its authors note that the design had been implanted in ten countries despite little published safety data [5]. Wikipedia describes BrightOcular as a silicone lens placed over the iris that can be removed later, and cites a French series of 87 eyes reporting frequent serious complications [1].

A separate body of surgical literature covers custom artificial iris prostheses for traumatic and congenital aniridia. A retrospective cohort of 51 patients who received a silicone artificial iris between 2011 and 2015 reported complications in about a quarter of cases, classified as mild, moderate or severe and managed with additional surgery [9]. These therapeutic series are distinct from cosmetic use in healthy eyes, but are cited in reviews as context for the device category.

Corneal tattooing, or keratopigmentation, has been used for centuries to mask corneal scars. Wikipedia traces it to Galen in about 150 AD, who used a heated stylet and dyes, with Aetius describing the same aim of masking white corneal opacities around 450 AD, and notes that Louis de Wecker introduced India ink in 1869 using a grooved needle [1]. Later surgeons added instruments: a bundle of needles (Taylor), an electric needle (Nieden, 1901) and a funnel device (Armaignac) [1].

In 2011 the ophthalmologist Jorge Alio combined the technique with a femtosecond laser to treat iris atrophy, and in 2014 to 2015 Francis Ferrari described aesthetic annular keratopigmentation for purely cosmetic color change in healthy eyes, sometimes called FLAAK (femtosecond laser aesthetic annular keratopigmentation) [1]. Wikipedia notes the cosmetic version has grown popular on social media and cites a 2024 Allure article reporting a price of about $12,000 [1].

In the femtosecond approach, a laser creates a tunnel or pocket within the corneal stroma and micronized pigment is placed there to form a ring of color over the iris. A 2025 narrative review reported that modern micronized pigments are biocompatible in histopathological studies, that most articles describe excellent outcomes and a high safety profile, and that more long-term studies are needed for strictly cosmetic use [2]. A 2025 updated review separating therapeutic from cosmetic use found that, in cosmetic cases, visual acuity tended to stay stable and the most frequently noted side effects were photophobia and ectasia, while fading and retouching were reported more often in therapeutic cases [3].

Pigments used historically and today include India ink and other carbon-based inks, and metallic salts such as gold or platinum chloride that produce a black stain but fade faster [1]. Wikipedia lists difficulty of precise execution, fading, shrinkage and the need for re-treatment among the disadvantages of tattooing in general, and keratitis, ulceration and granulomatous reactions among the serious risks [1].

Most keratopigmentation worldwide has been therapeutic: covering scarred or opaque corneas, improving the look of blind eyes, and reducing glare in aniridia, coloboma, iris atrophy and iridocorneal endothelial syndrome [1][2][10]. A 2025 series of eight eyes with opaque corneas used a manual two-plane technique, with brown pigment injected in a deeper pocket to imitate iris colour [11]. Reviews describe improved glare and sometimes improved visual acuity in patients who already had impaired vision, which is the setting where benefits are best documented [3][4].

A 2016 case series of patients who had BrightOcular implants placed solely for cosmetic reasons reported iritis, glaucoma and corneal decompensation [5], and a 2015 JAMA Ophthalmology report linked a newer cosmetic implant to corneal endothelial cell loss and iritis [12]. Case reports describe progressive corneal edema and glaucoma needing trabeculectomy and implant removal, and complications emerging 15 years after an uneventful procedure. The 2023 review attributes harms to mechanical irritation of angle structures, chronic inflammation, pigment dispersion and endothelial cell loss. Wikipedia's article on artificial irises lists raised eye pressure as the most common complication of such devices, along with misalignment and dislocation [8].

For laser keratopigmentation, a 2024 case series in Cornea described five patients (ten eyes) who developed progressive corneal ectasia between six months and four years after purely cosmetic femtosecond-laser keratopigmentation [13]. Reviews list photophobia and ectasia as the side effects most often reported after cosmetic procedures [3].

No controlled trials of cosmetic iris implants or keratopigmentation for eye color change were found. Evidence consists of case reports and case series [5][12][13], plus narrative reviews [2][3][4] and small therapeutic series on keratopigmentation, such as a study of eight eyes with opaque corneas treated with manual two-plane keratopigmentation [11]. Therapeutic artificial iris series, such as the 51-patient retrospective cohort, describe a different population from healthy eyes [9].

Tinted or iris-print contact lenses change apparent eye colour reversibly and are the usual comparison point in appearance forums, where posters note that a lens can leave a rim of brown visible when the pupil is smaller than the lens opening [6]. Wikipedia lists tinted contact lenses among the alternatives to corneal tattooing for scars as well [1].

On looksmax.org, threads discuss before-and-after images of eye color surgery, with some members saying they intend to have keratopigmentation because they have dark brown eyes and expect it to improve the eye area, others pointing to contact lenses as an alternative [6]. Another thread debates whether commenters on social media prefer the before pictures, with some posters describing results as unnatural on close-up, others saying that some results look good, and one remarking that the procedure may suit some eye shapes less than others [14]. A further thread discusses a reported case of vision loss after an eye color procedure, with members split between treating it as a warning and attributing it to the individual's delay in seeking care [15].

lore.intro: Members of appearance forums discuss eye color surgery as an option for people with dark eyes, comparing results photos and weighing it against colored contact lenses [14][6][15].
